full_judgment:
5. The prosecution examined seven witnesses all of whom were cross-examined by the defence. After close of the prosecution witnesses, the accused was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which he reported his innocence. The defence did not adduce any evidence. 

 7. The learned Tribunal thereafter in consideration of evidence on record as well as facts and circumstance of the case. However found the accused appellant guilty for the offence charged and convicted him thereunder and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for two years and also ordered to pay a fine of Tk. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for three months. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied thereby the accused as appellant has come up with the present appeal which is opposed by the respondent State through the learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Md. Mahmood Hossain. 

 8. Mr. Taimur Alam Khandaker, the learned Advocate for the appellant took us through the evidence on record, impugned judgment F.I.R. seizure list, charge sheet and other relevant papers as available on record and submits that this is a case of no evidence, but the learned trial Court found the accused guilty on guess and surmise. He incidentally submits that the seizure list witnesses did not support the prosecution case and as such he contends that the impugned judgment, order of conviction and sentences passed thereunder is liable to be set side. 

 9. Mr. Md. Mahmood Hossain learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondent State opposes the appeal contending inter alia that the prosecution has successfully proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, though the private witnesses for obvious reason did not support the prosecution case. He finally submits that the overall evidence of the private P.Ws. indicates that they being gained over by the accused have tried to evade from speaking the truth and their admitted fact indicates that the recovery took place in their presence inasmuch as they admitted their signatures on the seizure list as well as presence at the time of alleged seizure but for reason best known to them claimed that they did not see the recovery but failed to state as to why they signed on the seizure list which was prepared after seizure of the incriminating articles in question. 

 13. P.W. 7 the Investigating Officer said about investigation of the case. He gave the history of his investigation in details and nothing transpires against the prosecution about his investigation during cross. This is all about the evidence on record. 

 14. The critical analysis of the aforesaid evidence clearly indicates that the seizure of the incriminating articles have been proved by the official witnesses who were allegedly on patrol duty on the date, but the private witnesses who did not support the prosecution case. Mr. Taimur Alam Khandaker, the learned Advocate for the appellant referred to a decision reported in V.B. L. C. (2000) 703, in the case of Musa Mia Vs. The State and submits that the seizure list witnesses have not supported the prosecution case of recovery when the evidence of Habilder a member of raiding party made the recovery of the incriminating articles when none on the neighbours were called at the time of recovery, the prosecution has failed to prove the alleged recovery of the incriminating articles beyond reasonable doubt. We have carefully gone through the aforesaid decision and reasons to believe that the facts and circumstance of the present case is clearly distinguishable from the present one because in the instant case the seizure list witnesses did not deny their presence on the date as well as their signatures on the seizure list, but simply claimed that no incriminating articles were seized in their presence but in the reported case none of the seizure list witnesses turned up nor admitted their signatures on the seizure list. So the decision so referred to above is of no help to the appellant. In the instant case it is evident that the members of raiding party including the informant who are none but members of law enforcing agency have said about recovery of the incriminating articles from the control and possession of the accused appellant. There is distinction between a case in which prosecution may be enable to produce the seizure list witnesses on the ground that they have been gained over by the accused. Recovery would be proved by solitary statement of investigating officer and such officer was to be treated to be as good witness as any other member of public, particularly, when such officer was not shown to have had a motive to falsely involve the accused. In the instant case P.W. 1 the informant and P.W.2 another member of law enforcing agency who had accompanied P.W. 1 on the date of occurrence have categorically said about recovery of incriminating articles from the control and possession of the accused appellant and the defence has failed to show that they had any reason of enmity to depose against him (accused appellant). Furthermore, the admission of the signatures by the seizure list witnesses P.Ws. 5 and 6 on the seizure list clearly justify their some unnatural behaviour on this point, because they admitted their signatures on the seizure list and failed to state as to why they signed their names thereto without seeing the seizure of the incriminating articles. Furthermore, the remained meticulously silent as to why they went to place of occurrence at an odd hour of night. 

 15. Mr. Taimur Alam Khandaker, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that provisions of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been complied in this case and as such the benefit must go in favour of his client. Admittedly the incriminating articles were recovered in a raid conducted by a police officer on the basis of a secret information. When a raiding party is constituted then this section cannot be applied with the latter. Because if the attempt is made, then the entire mission comes out and the other party is likely to get to know it. So as to due why with the stolen property which is intended to be recovered therefrom in raid cases witnesses are generally taken from the place where a raiding party is formed. The provision of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure apply only when search is made under Chapter VII of the Code. These provisions do not apply to a case of apprehension of persons suspected to be carrying any intoxicant, or any other nothing liable to be confiscation under the law. The incriminating articles of the present case are, no doubt, intoxicated element and as such we are of opinion that the compliance of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not necessary. On the other hand, it appears that the members of raiding party have proved the recovery of the incriminating articles from the control and possession of the accused appellant and the private witnesses admitted their signatures over the seizure list, but did not supported their knowledge about seizure of the incriminating articles in their presence without any explanation as to why they signed in the seizure list without seeing the incriminating articles. In view of such facts and circumstances we are led to hold that the learned Tribunal has rightly found that the prosecution has successfully proved the recovery of the incriminating articles from the control and possession of the accused appellant and as such the same deserves no interference by this Court.
